prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs boson at rank 1 because it is the discovery nature delivered most unambiguously, but the opening ballots show that the discovery-first criterion is met by B052 with far fewer attribution problems. Optical lattice clocks follow a clear chain: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstration, then Ye's realisation of record accuracy and stability. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) now agree at the 10^-18 level, which is exactly the kind of replication I want before asking who deserves credit. The consequences reach beyond metrology: gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a candidate redefinition of the second. That gives a clue from nature, not just an elegant instrument. Eight of eight members ranked it, which tells me it is the one candidate no colleague finds unreasonable, and the two-name credit is clean. If the committee wants a prize that is defensible on both discovery and attribution, this is the strongest configuration on the table.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one I raised myself at rank 4: this may be read as an advance in instrumentation rather than a discovery, and the frequency comb (2005) and ion-trap (2012) prizes already covered much of the metrological narrative. Ranking it first risks rewarding what is a superb measurement tool before it has produced a decisive new physical result, since no variation of constants or dark-matter signal has appeared. There is also a risk that I am retreating from the Higgs, a genuinely foundational discovery that has never been recognised on the experimental side, merely because its attribution is hard. Difficulty of attribution is a problem for the committee, not a verdict on the science, and I do not want to let a statute limit of three people decide what counts as important.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the Higgs observation second but warned that Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are founding leaders rather than the people who made the decisive 2012 measurement, and that leadership should not be treated as equivalent to discovery.
responses.response: I agree and I should have weighted this more heavily in my own opening, where I only called the attribution imperfect. The people who actually announced the signal were the 2012 spokespersons, trigger and analysis leaders, and the credited three do not map onto them. A prize that credits instrument founders for a physics observation would invite exactly the leadership-versus-discovery dispute Eva describes. This is what moves the Higgs from my first choice to an alternative. I would still rather the committee reached for it than abandon it, but it needs a citation and a name set that we can actually defend.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked the Higgs only seventh and noted that the committee historically avoids leader-based awards for large collaborations, that spokespersons and accelerator builders are outside the credited list, and that the 2013 prize can be seen as having already honoured the Higgs.
responses.response: I take the first two points seriously and they have shifted me, but I resist the third. The 2013 prize honoured a prediction, and the experimental discovery of a scalar at 125 GeV is a separate act of nature being read out, which is precisely why I put it first. Bernhard's point about committee practice is the real obstacle, though, and I do not see a three-name answer that is both fair and true to the record. Where I differ is that a hard allocation problem is not a reason to rank the physics low, so I would keep it as a live alternative rather than treat it as closed.

responses.point: Kroll put optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed, with high originality, clarity and breadth, in the tradition of the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and with the two-person allocation, and I now see it as my preferred outcome. My difference with Stefan is one of emphasis: I would want the citation to point to what clocks have shown (redshift across millimetres, constraints on constants), not just that they are more accurate, to answer the objection that this is engineering. I also think we should be candid that Ye's name appears on the thorium nuclear clock candidate, so the citation should be bounded to lattice clocks and not become a prize for the whole of precision spectroscopy.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked IceCube first as an instrument-plus-discovery result that opened a new window, with Halzen and Spiering as a clean two-name credit, though earlier AMANDA and Baikal pioneers raise a fairness question.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube second and I still think it is the most natural astroparticle choice, so I do not dispute Mark's case for it. Where I part from him is on maturity: the diffuse flux is solid, but the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are still few and at moderate significance, so a citation resting on them is early, and one resting on the diffuse flux alone sells the result short. I would also press the pioneer question harder than he does, since Spiering's AMANDA and Baikal lineage and the DUMAND history are not in the credited set. I think IceCube is a strong candidate for a few years from now and a reasonable alternative today.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as a discovery or as instrumentation, given the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether a three-name set can fairly represent the ATLAS and CMS Higgs observation, and whether any citation could solve this.
Whether IceCube source associations will strengthen enough to make B043 the better choice, and how to handle the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers.
I am recalling lattice-clock priority details (Katori versus other early lattice-clock groups, and Ye's role) from memory and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration: my ties are to my PhD supervisor David Gross, the late Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, none of whom relate to B052, B010 or B043. B041 (Event Horizon Telescope) lies close to my own horizonless black-hole mimicker work, so I would be careful about that candidate and would raise it if it came to a vote.
